headline: AI pioneer Andrew Ng said there is no meaningful risk of AI wiping out humanity and accused some companies of using "made-up safety arguments" to push rules that stifle competition.
score_reason: A prominent researcher's contrarian claim about industry motives, made on a podcast published 13 Oct; his view, not a finding. Lowered from 6 because the interview is two days old.
importance_line: The debate over whether AI rules protect people or protect big companies is shaping regulation, but Ng's claim about motives is his opinion and the named companies were not quoted in reply.
summary: The New York Post reports that Andrew Ng, co-founder of Google's Brain project and of the online-learning firm Coursera, told The Economist's "Inside Tech" podcast, published on 13 Oct 2026, that he sees "no meaningful human existential risks from AI" and that a handful of businesses lobbied with made-up safety arguments to get rules that crush competition. His remarks are widely read as a reply to the recent calls by Anthropic's Dario Amodei, OpenAI's Sam Altman and Elon Musk to slow AI; he also said recursive self-improvement is "much more hype than reality" and called the OpenAI agents' breach of Hugging Face "an engineering problem to be solved".
notes: TOI page empty; read the New York Post's report of the Economist podcast. The reply link to Amodei, Altman and Musk comes from the TOI headline and the surrounding debate; the Post does not name them as addressees, so it is written as 'widely read as'. Score lowered 6 to 5: event 13 Oct.
